query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of aluminum to the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C.
generation.mechanism: aluminum addition reduces density while maintaining mechanical properties due to its low density and potential to form a stable solid solution
generation.predicted_outcome: reduced density without significant loss of mechanical properties
generation.baseline: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g/cm³
generation.boundary: temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C, loading: not specified
generation.uncertainty: effect of aluminum addition on high-temperature oxidation resistance and potential for phase instability

falsification_experiment.design: prepare HfMoTaTiZr alloys with varying aluminum content, measure density and mechanical properties at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the addition of aluminum results in a significant loss of mechanical properties (e.g., >10% reduction in yield strength or ultimate tensile strength) at room temperature or 1000 °C, the hypothesis is falsified

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ]. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) has been focused on improving their mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, while reducing their density. Various processing techniques, including vacuum induction melting, directional solidification, and additive manufacturing, have been explored to achieve these goals. The addition of alloying elements, such as hafnium and molybdenum, has also been investigated to enhance the properties of HEAs. Furthermore, the use of reinforcement particles, such as TiC and Al2O3, has been shown to improve the compressive strength of HEAs.
